input_artifacts: user prompt (research topic and length request)

selected_rq: Within U.S. electric power generation (NAICS 2211), how large are the hourly wage gaps between renewable generation industries (solar, wind, hydroelectric, geothermal, biomass) and non-renewable generation industries (fossil fuel and nuclear), do these gaps persist within detailed occupations, how do they differ across individual energy sources and occupational groups, and how did they change between 2021 and 2025?
directional_relation: Competing expectations: a green-premium account predicts renewable > non-renewable within occupation; a legacy rent-sharing account predicts renewable < non-renewable, with nuclear highest and hydro closest to fossil; the gap is expected to narrow over 2021-2025 if renewable segments mature.
mechanism: Legacy fossil and nuclear generation is a mature, capital-intensive, heavily regulated and comparatively unionized segment with large incumbent firms and rent-sharing, whereas the newer solar and wind segments are younger, more contractor- and developer-based, less unionized and have flatter internal labor markets; establishment wage-setting rather than occupational skill should therefore produce within-occupation wage gaps that may narrow as renewable segments mature and as IRA prevailing-wage provisions take effect.
confounders: skill and education requirements embedded in occupations
geographic location of plants (not observable nationally)
firm size and union coverage (not observable)

scope.population: occupation-by-industry employment cells in U.S. electric power generation (NAICS 2211, eight six-digit generation industries)
scope.unit: detailed SOC occupation x six-digit generation industry x year cell

target_journal.fit_rationale: Just-transition wage implications of the shift from fossil to renewable generation are core to the journal's policy audience; the design is transparent and policy-relevant.
target_journal.method_bar: transparent descriptive regression design with occupation-by-year fixed effects, employment weights, clustered errors, decomposition, and robustness to sampling error and sector definitions
target_journal.theory_bar: clear statement of competing green-premium versus legacy-rent mechanisms and explicit scope limits
desk_reject_risks: perceived as purely descriptive without policy hook
OEWS cell data lack worker controls

method_orientation: observational quantitative panel of repeated occupation-by-industry cross-sections
recommended_dataset: BLS Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics (OEWS) national industry-specific estimates, May 2021-May 2025, NAICS 221111-221118
rationale: Policy debates assume the clean-energy transition creates better-paid jobs, yet the strongest evidence compares broad green and non-green jobs. Comparing the same occupations across generation sources within one industry shows whether workers moving from fossil plants to solar or wind farms face pay cuts, and how this changed during the IRA period.

selection_evidence.exploratory_signal_note: Exploratory bivariate check (not causal): within occupation-year, renewable cells average roughly 12 log points below non-renewable cells; used only for feasibility.

x_detail: renewable (solar, wind, hydroelectric, geothermal, biomass) versus non-renewable (fossil fuel, nuclear) six-digit generation industry, and each individual generation source
y_detail: log real mean hourly wage (2025 dollars) of detailed occupation-industry cells
